title: Solve common coding and DSA interview problems in a finance context: sliding window, two pointers, HashMap lookup, dynamic programming, and tree and graph traversal: and explain the pattern and complexity of each.
shortTitle: Coding/DSA: sliding window, two pointers, HashMap, DP, trees, graphs (finance context)
keyPoints: Sliding window tracks a moving range over an array and updates a running result in O(n) time without recomputing from scratch.
HashMap gives O(1) average lookup, turning O(n squared) brute-force pair searches into O(n) single-pass scans.
Two pointers on sorted data find pairs summing to a target in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.
Dynamic programming builds optimal answers from smaller overlapping subproblems using a table, such as minimum notes for an ATM withdrawal.
DFS and BFS traverse trees and graphs in O(V + E) time and detect cycles, levels, and shortest paths.
Always state time and space complexity out loud in an interview and use BigDecimal for money, never double.
Each pattern is a reusable template: recognising which one fits a problem is the first and most important step.

s1_definition.oneliner: Pick the pattern that matches the problem – sliding window for subarrays, HashMap for lookups, DFS/BFS for graphs and trees, DP for optimization – and always state the time and space complexity.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **DSA patterns** – a small set of reusable algorithmic templates that cover most coding interview problems.
- **Sliding window** – maintains a moving range over an array and updates a running result as the window slides, avoiding full recomputation.
- **Two pointers** – uses two index variables on sorted data to find pairs or compact elements in a single linear pass.
- **HashMap lookup** – trades O(n) space for O(1) average-time lookups, reducing brute-force pair searches from quadratic to linear.
- **Dynamic programming** – builds optimal answers bottom-up from overlapping subproblems stored in a table.
- **Graph traversal (DFS/BFS)** – explores nodes and edges in O(V + E) time to detect cycles, compute levels, or find shortest paths.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the back office at the National Bank of India drowning in data: daily stock prices, lists of transactions, account hierarchies, and transfer networks. DSA patterns are the smart shortcuts the clerks use instead of brute force. The sliding window is like a clerk sliding a ruler across a row of daily prices to spot the best buy-and-sell window without re-reading the whole row each time. A HashMap is like an index card box where the clerk instantly finds a matching amount instead of flipping through every slip. Depth-first search is like following a chain of transfers to see if the money loops back, which would signal fraud.

sections.s6_takeaway:
For coding interviews I always start by identifying which pattern the problem matches, because the right pattern is the difference between an elegant linear solution and a brute-force one that times out. The core patterns I rely on are the sliding window for subarray and substring problems, the HashMap for constant-time lookup, two pointers for sorted pair searches, dynamic programming for overlapping subproblems, and DFS/BFS for tree and graph traversal. Each pattern has a characteristic time and space cost, and stating that cost out loud for every solution is what separates a senior answer from a junior one.

In my work at the National Bank of India I apply these patterns to real financial data daily. The sliding window computes moving averages and finds the best buy-and-sell window on stock prices. The HashMap detects suspicious transaction pairs that sum to a flagged target. Two pointers find matching settlement amounts in a sorted ledger. DP powers the ATM dispenser that minimises the number of notes for a withdrawal. DFS detects circular transfer chains that may indicate money laundering.

The habits that make me look senior are always using BigDecimal for money instead of double, handling edge cases like empty input and no valid answer before the main logic, and structuring each algorithm as a self-contained class with clear single responsibility. I also know the trade-offs: HashMap trades memory for speed, DP trades memory to avoid recomputation, and two pointers avoids both extras by requiring sorted input.

Every pattern is a reusable template. Once I recognise which one fits, the implementation follows naturally. The interview is really testing whether I can see the pattern in a new problem, not whether I can memorise code. That recognition skill comes from practising the templates until they are second nature.

Remember one sentence: identify the DSA pattern first, code the template second, and always state the time and space complexity out loud.
